description_full: Occidental Petroleum Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the acquisition, exploration, and development of oil and gas properties in the United States and internationally. It operates through Oil and Gas and Midstream and Marketing. The Oil and Gas segment explores for, develops, and produces oil and condensate, natural gas liquids (NGLs), and natural gas. This segment also optimizes its transportation and storage capacity and invests in entities. The Midstream and Marketing segment purchases, markets, gathers, processes, transports and stores oil, condensate, NGLs, natural gas, carbon dioxide, and power. Occidental Petroleum Corporation was founded in 1920 and is headquartered in Houston, Texas.

financial_summary: Occidental Petroleum Corporatio is a large-cap energy business with a $58.7B market cap on $21.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -16% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $4.1B in free cash flow — roughly 19 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 6.53× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 3.9×.

Net dilution runs at 0.0% annually, transferring value from owners to stock-based comp, and insiders hold 27% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sector_headwinds.text: Altman Z in the distress zone (1.5) — the kind of balance-sheet risk that can make a loss permanent
Revenue growth in the bottom decile of Energy peers — losing share inside the profit pool

Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Piotroski score 4/9 — below the median for a healthy business
The commodity cycle — revenue and free cash flow are ultimately hostage to a price the company does not set, and the long-run energy-transition arc adds a structural overhang.
ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.

growth: Revenue has compounded at -16.2% over 3 years, 3.9% over 5 years and 5.6% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 25%).
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 23.7% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 29.8% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 22, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 62.3% on average.
own: Insiders own 26.8%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 59%.

people: With about 10,412 employees, each generates about $2.1M of revenue, in line with the Energy median, and revenue has grown 2.1% a year across its filed history.

CEO pay is $2.3M (1x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
